n: Walking through Jerusalem, Jesus notices a man who has been blind since birth. Jesus sees him first — the man doesn’t ask for help.

f.g: John stresses this detail; healing congenital blindness was unheard of (see verse 32).

n: The disciples voice a common belief that suffering is punishment for sin, and wonder whose sin caused this — his own, or his parents’?

f.w: who did sin, this man, or his parents

n: Jesus rejects the blame game. This blindness isn’t punishment; it is an opportunity for God’s work to be displayed in the man’s life.

f.w: that the works of God should be made manifest in him
f.g: manifest = shown openly.

n: Jesus feels urgency: he must do his Father’s work while the daylight of his mortal ministry lasts, for the night of his death is coming.

f.w: the night cometh, when no man can work

n: While he is in the world, he is its light — and he is about to demonstrate it by giving sight to a blind man.

f.w: I am the light of the world

n: Jesus spits on the ground, makes mud, and spreads it on the man’s eyes. Some see a link to God forming man from the dust; the act also gave a blind man something to feel and do.

f.g: anointed = smeared, applied.

n: Jesus sends him to wash in the Pool of Siloam, whose name means “Sent.” The man obeys in faith, washes, and comes back able to see.

f.g: A pool at the south end of Jerusalem fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel; its remains have been excavated.
Jesus himself is repeatedly called the one “sent” by the Father in John.

n: His neighbors and those who knew him as a beggar are stunned and ask whether this is really the same man.

f.g: With few other options, blind people often begged near the temple or city gates.

n: Some say yes, others think it must be a look-alike; the man himself insists, “I am he.”

f.g: He uses the same Greek phrase, egō eimi, that Jesus uses of himself, though here simply meaning “It’s me.”

n: So they ask him how his eyes were opened.

f.g: This question is asked repeatedly in the chapter (verses 15, 19, 26).

n: He tells the simple facts: “a man called Jesus” made mud, told him to wash, and now he sees. At this point he knows little about Jesus — watch his understanding grow.

f.w: A man that is called Jesus
f.g: His view of Jesus grows: a man (v. 11), a prophet (v. 17), from God (v. 33), Lord to be worshipped (v. 38).

n: Asked where Jesus is, he admits he doesn’t know.

f.g: He had never seen Jesus — he was still blind when Jesus sent him away.

n: The neighbors bring the formerly blind man to the Pharisees, the religious experts.

f.g: aforetime = previously.

n: John adds the crucial detail: it was the Sabbath. Kneading clay and healing a non-life-threatening condition broke the rabbis’ Sabbath rules.
The Pharisees question him, and he briefly repeats what happened.

f.g: His account gets shorter as the questioning goes on.

n: The Pharisees split: some say Jesus can’t be from God since he broke the Sabbath; others ask how a sinner could do such miracles.
They ask the man’s opinion, and he declares boldly that Jesus is a prophet.
The leaders refuse to believe the man was ever blind until they summon his parents.

f.g: Unbelief here is a choice not to accept the evidence.

n: They ask the parents three things: is this your son, was he born blind, and how does he now see?

f.w: how then doth he now see?
f.g: doth = does.

n: The parents confirm he is their son and was born blind.

f.g: They will testify only to what is safe.

n: But they carefully avoid saying how he was healed or by whom, telling the leaders to ask their adult son himself.

f.g: He is an adult, legally able to testify for himself (thirteen or older under Jewish custom).

n: John explains: the parents were afraid, because the leaders had decided that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Messiah would be expelled from the synagogue.

f.g: Expulsion meant being cut off from community worship and social life.

n: That fear is why they pass the question back to their son.

f.g: Their caution contrasts with their son’s growing courage.

n: Recalling the man, the leaders order him to “give God the praise” — an oath formula meaning “tell the truth before God” — and declare that Jesus is a sinner.

f.g: A solemn charge to confess the truth, as Joshua said to Achan.

n: His answer is one of the great testimonies in scripture: he can’t settle theological debates, but he knows one thing — he was blind, and now he sees.

f.w: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see

n: They ask again how Jesus opened his eyes, hoping to catch a contradiction.

f.g: They are looking for evidence of Sabbath-breaking.

n: Exasperated, he says he already told them. Then, with sharp irony, he asks whether they want to become Jesus’s disciples too.

f.w: will ye also be his disciples?
f.g: The word “also” hints he already thinks of himself as a disciple.

n: They heap insults on him: he can be Jesus’s disciple, but they are disciples of Moses.

f.g: reviled = abused with insulting words.

n: They know God spoke to Moses, they say, but they don’t know where this fellow comes from.
The man marvels: the experts can’t tell where Jesus comes from, yet Jesus opened his eyes. Isn’t the answer obvious?

f.g: An amazing thing — he is gently mocking their blindness.

n: He reasons from common belief: God doesn’t answer the prayers of the wicked, but listens to those who worship him and do his will.
Never in history has anyone given sight to a person born blind. Something divine has happened.
His conclusion: if Jesus weren’t from God, he could do nothing at all.

f.w: If this man were not of God

n: Unable to answer, they insult him as someone born steeped in sin and throw him out. The man has lost his community for telling the truth.

f.g: Probably expelled from the synagogue, as threatened in verse 22.

n: Jesus hears about it and seeks the man out. The Good Shepherd finds the one who was cast out and asks if he believes in the Son of God.

f.g: Many early manuscripts read “Son of man.”

n: He is eager: tell me who he is, Lord, so I can believe in him.

f.g: Here probably “Sir,” though the word deepens in meaning by verse 38.

n: Jesus reveals himself: you have seen him — the very one now speaking with you. For a man born blind, “you have seen him” carries special joy.

f.w: it is he that talketh with thee

n: The man believes and worships Jesus. His journey from physical sight to spiritual sight is complete.
Jesus explains the result of his coming: those who know they are blind receive sight, while those who think they see are shown to be blind.

f.w: that they which see not might see

n: Some Pharisees nearby bristle: surely he doesn’t mean they are blind?
If they admitted their blindness, they could be healed. But claiming to see while rejecting the light leaves their sin in place. Pride blocks the cure.

f.w: If ye were blind, ye should have no sin
